problem: Synthetic instruction-trajectory data for VLN is large-scale but low-fidelity: training on 4.9M ScaleVLN pairs (SPL 50.1) or 1M Prevalent pairs (SPL 54.8) is worse than training on 14K human R2R (SPL 55.9). Existing scorers such as CLIP-score cannot judge multi-scene directional and semantic alignment.
motivation: Human annotation is too expensive to scale, and simply adding more environments or instructions does not help when the language is noisy and low in vocabulary diversity. A trained navigator already links landmarks and directions to actions, so its ability to re-follow a generated instruction can measure instruction-trajectory alignment. This turns instruction-trajectory similarity into a simpler trajectory-trajectory similarity.
key_idea: Run a self-refining data flywheel in which a navigator filters generated instructions by re-following them (nDTW/SPL against the source path), the filtered data trains a better MLLM instruction generator, and the better generator re-labels the rejected data to train a stronger navigator, repeated over rounds.
insight: Navigator-based nDTW filtering is far better than CLIP-Sim, Mantis-score or self-score for selecting good instructions. It gives SPICE 25.4 vs 23.7 with no filter, and 25.2 vs 23.6-23.9 for round-2 generators trained on filtered data. Instruction quality also determines whether diversity helps: with our instructions the navigator keeps improving up to 6 instructions per path, while Prevalent saturates at 3. Ablations show that the interleaved image-action prompt matters (SPICE-D 28.4 vs 24.4 image-only) and that the flywheel is not tied to Mantis (it also helps mPLUG-Owl).
method: Base instruction generator: Mantis-8B-SigLIP (LLaMA-3) with LoRA fine-tuned on R2R using an interleaved image-action trajectory prompt (arrival and departure views at each viewpoint, each followed by a text action such as 'left 33 degree' or 'forward').

Data generation: the generator produces greedy-decoded instructions (D^G, high confidence, used to train the next generator) and sampled top-3/top-5 instructions (D^N, diverse, used to train the navigator) for unlabeled MP3D (178K) and HM3D (2.89M) trajectories.
Navigator (DUET): pre-trained on D^N with MLM and single action prediction, then fine-tuned on R2R. It serves as the evaluator and the final agent.

Navigator-as-filter: the navigator re-runs each generated instruction. Greedy data is kept if SPL=1, giving FD^G, and sampled data is kept if nDTW>=0.9. Only the rejected samples are re-generated in the next round, so the total data size is fixed.
Iterative loop: in each round, train G_t on FD^G_t, re-generate the low-quality navigator data with G_t, retrain the navigator N_t, and re-filter. Both models are initialized from the previous round.
Final dataset SRDF-20M: 20.4M instructions, 860 environments, 10,363 vocabulary words, plus 0.9M filtered greedy data FD^G_4. FD^G_4 is used for R2R fine-tuning and for a final round-4 generator.
Downstream transfer: the pre-trained navigator is fine-tuned on R2R, RxR-en, R4R, CVDN, REVERIE and SOON with PanoGen/ScaleVLN/Marky augmentation, and on R2R-CE via ETPNav with CLIP-B/16.

results: After three flywheel rounds, the DUET navigator reaches 78 SPL / 85 SR on R2R test, surpassing human performance (76 SPL) and the strongest baseline ScaleVLN (70 SPL). Val-unseen SPL rises through rounds from 75.9 to 77.3 to 77.6 in the InternViT-feature ablation setting, and the generator's SPICE rises from 21.8 (EnvDrop) to 26.2. The pre-trained navigator also sets new state of the art on R2R-CE (SR 65 vs 61), RxR-en, R4R (SR 64.4 vs 47.8), CVDN, REVERIE and SOON.
limitations: Depends on a reasonably strong seed navigator and generator, and the gains rely on very large compute (a 6B InternViT encoder, 20M pre-training instructions).
Filtering requires nDTW/SPL agreement with the sampled path, so it may favor easy shortest-path-like trajectories, and improvements diminish over rounds (+0.3 SPL in round 3).
Evaluated only on discrete-graph VLN with R2R-style seed data and MP3D/HM3D environments; no real-robot experiments.
